english: Let $F:\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that $F(0)=0$ and $F'(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x+\sqrt3\cos x}$ for all $x\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$. Let $\theta\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ be such that $F(\theta)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\log_{e}\dfrac{5+3\sqrt3}{2}$. Then the value of $\dfrac{180\,\theta}{\pi}$ is ______.

$F'>0$, so $\theta$ is unique. Try $t=\sqrt3$ ($\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$): $\dfrac{(\sqrt3+1)(2+\sqrt3)}{2}=\dfrac{5+3\sqrt3}{2}$, which matches
solution_full: Put $t=\tan\dfrac x2$, so $\sin x=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^{2}}$, $\cos x=\dfrac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}$, $dx=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}$. For $x\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$, $\dfrac x2\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\right)$ and $t\in(-1,2+\sqrt3)$.

The quadratic is the half-angle form of the equation $\sin x+\sqrt3\cos x=-1$. Its roots are $t=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-4(1-3)}}{2(1-\sqrt3)}=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt3}{1-\sqrt3}$, i.e. $t=-1$ and $t=2+\sqrt3$; these are $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, the ends of the domain (equivalently $2\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-1$).

The denominator $1+2\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is positive on the domain, so $F$ is strictly increasing and $\theta$ is unique. The equation becomes $\dfrac{(t+1)(2+\sqrt3)}{2+\sqrt3-t}=\dfrac{5+3\sqrt3}{2}$.
originality_note: New: the domain of F is exactly the interval between consecutive solutions of sin x + sqrt3 cos x = -1, which appear as the roots of the half-angle quadratic; the antiderivative is a single log and the angle at which it reaches a given value is recovered (way 5). Closest known: textbook integrals 1/(a sin x + b cos x + c) via t = tan(x/2). Different because: the solution of the trigonometric equation in half-angle form gives the factorisation, and the question inverts the antiderivative.
key_step: Factoring the half-angle quadratic (1-sqrt3)t^2 + 2t + (1+sqrt3) with roots -1 and 2+sqrt3, integrating to a single log, and inverting at tan(theta/2) = sqrt3.
justification: Two linked ideas: solving the trigonometric equation by the half-angle substitution to factor the denominator, then a partial-fraction log antiderivative that must be inverted, with surd arithmetic and no options. Comparable to 2025-P2-Q3 (L3) trig-equation question and 2023-P2-Q8 (L3).
